extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; advanced creative writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and deliberate use of the narrating instance: its temporal relation to the story (subsequent/prior/simultaneous/interpolated), its duration, tense choices, and the narrative-level (extradiegetic/diegetic/metadiegetic) structure and their effects on meaning and focalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal determination of the narrating (time of the narrating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief temporal determination of the narrating instance is its position relative to the story; the narrating must be located in time (present, past, or future tense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is more important than spatial determination: while place can be unspecified, narrating is almost always temporally located by tense. Temporal position shapes significance (e.g., Proust's long interval between a scene and its evocation is essential to meaning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four types of narrating by temporal position
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate four types of narrating: subsequent (classical past-tense narrative), prior (predictive narrative), simultaneous (present-tense contemporaneous narrative), and interpolated (narrating inserted between moments of the action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type carries distinct effects and analytic challenges: subsequent is most frequent; prior appears mainly in second-degree narratives; simultaneous can produce objectivity or intensify discourse (interior monologue); interpolated involves multiple instances and can entangle story and narrating (epistolary and journal forms). Examples: Wuthering Heights (journal), Moyse sauve (prophetic passages), Rebecca/Vanity Fair (simultaneous report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of present tense (narrative present)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present tense can connote temporal indefiniteness and can be used for simultaneousness, but also has ambivalent effects: it may promote transparency/objectivity (story-focused) or emphasize the narrating/discourse (interior monologue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present-tense narrative was associated with the French 'new novel' and writers like Robbe-Grillet (objectivity) or Dujardin/Beckett (interior monologue); certain uses of present tense are reserved for jokes, riddles, scientific problems, plot summaries, and may have preterite value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive (prior) narrative as a distinct strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictive narratives are those where the narrating precedes the story (prophetic, apocalyptic, oracular, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive narrative has limited literary investment in many traditions and often occurs on a second level (e.g., Aaron's prophecy or Jocabel's dream in Moyse sauve). Some 'anticipation' novels still implicitly postdate their narrating instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolated narrating: complexity and narrating-as-event
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolated narrating (narrating inserted between moments of the action) involves several narrating instances and may make the narrating an event that affects the story (common in epistolary novels and journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type is analytically complex and refractory: letters/journals combine live and prerecorded accounts, mix 'quasi-interior monologue' and 'account after the event', and can produce multiple successive hypostases of a character (the hero of yesterday vs narrator of today). Examples: Manon Lescaut, L'Etranger, Les Liaisons dangereuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent narrating and the fiction of atemporality
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent narrating (past-tense) is usually treated in the text as instantaneous and atemporal—although in reality the writing may take years, the narrative presents the narrating as a single moment without duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fiction of instantaneous narrating is a powerful literary device. The past tense situates narrating after the story but typically does not measure the interval; exceptions (passé composé, present tense) can connote relative closeness or living connection to the present. Examples: Proust (Recherche) treated as instantaneous narrating despite long real writing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of narrating as a formal variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Different narrating types exist through their duration and their relation to story time: simultaneous or interpolated narrating reveal duration and relations to story, while subsequent narrating is paradoxically atemporal in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duration (or lack of it) of the narrating instance affects how the reader perceives causal/temporal relations and dramatic effects (e.g., Tristram Shandy's problem of narrating time vs lived time; broadcasting/live-reporting parallels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative levels: extradiegetic, diegetic, metadiegetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Any event a narrative recounts is at a diegetic level immediately higher than the level at which the narrating act producing this narrative is placed: extradiegetic (first-level narrator addressing the public), diegetic/intradiegetic (events told inside that narrative), metadiegetic (a narrative within the narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these level terms to map framing relations and embedded narratives: e.g., M. de Renoncourt's Memoires are extradiegetic; Des Grieux's account within them is diegetic/intradiegetic and Des Grieux's own narrated episodes are metadiegetic. The terms designate relative situations/functions, not individuals; levels can be nested to any degree (meta-metanarrative, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictive vs real authorship and narrating function
rubrics_metrics.description: Extradiegetic status does not imply real historical existence: fictive authors/narrators can function as extradiegetic narrating instances addressing the actual public; conversely, diary/epistolary forms may not intend a public and their fictive authors may present themselves as 'editors', not authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate extradiegetic with real-world authorship. The nature of the narrating medium (written, oral, interior monologue, transcribed speech) affects whether the narrating is formally determined as a written act; e.g., interior monologue may be presented as a transcribed speech with no formal narrating-instance determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of narrating (oral, written, interior monologue, work-within-a-work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intradiegetic narrating can be oral or written, and may itself produce a fictive literary text (a work within a work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Des Grieux's oral account, Adolphe's written memoir, Don Quixote's 'Curious Impertinent' as a discovered story, or Albert Savarus's fictive published novella. The medium chosen changes performative and diegetic relations: a letter as both narrative medium and plot element (performative letters in Les Liaisons dangereuses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator/hero relations and final convergence (asymptote)
rubrics_metrics.description: In first-person/autobiographical modes the narrator is presented as a character; the hero may approach but not fully coincide with the narrator—the interval may shrink (final convergence) but often remains an asymptote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative typically halts when the hero becomes (or begins to become) the narrator; the Bildungsroman's 'continuation' (the life after vocation) is non-novelistic and may be only sketched. Examples: Proust's Recherche where hero becomes writer but the narrative stops before full merger; exceptions in some picaresque works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal pacing techniques to signal changing narrator-story distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify temporal pacing (disappearance of the iterative, lengthening of singulative scenes, increasing discontinuity, accentuation of rhythm) to make the shrinking interval between story time and narrating time felt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust employed these techniques to convey the approach of the story toward the narrating moment; such micro-temporal devices can create perceived dilation or contraction of story time relative to narrating time and produce significance beyond tense alone.
